data.sentence: Alright, let's get started — this is the review of Tuesday's game day on the Detect ingestion pipeline.
Ravi ran the scenarios, so I'll let him walk through them, and then I want to land on what's left before we call the reliability work done.
Sure. We ran five scenarios in the staging cluster at about one point two times our current peak event volume.
Scenario one was killing the primary ingestion node outright. Failover completed in eleven seconds and we lost zero events.
That's better than the fourteen we saw in the sprint retro.
Yeah, tuning the health check interval helped. Scenario two was memory pressure — the exact failure mode from March.
The circuit breaker tripped at eighty-five percent memory, shed load to the secondary, and the primary recovered on its own.
So the thing that took us down for six hours now just... recovers. That's huge.
Scenario three is where we found something. We partitioned the network between the queue and the processing nodes.
Both nodes stayed healthy but stopped receiving events, and our alerting didn't fire for about six minutes.
Six minutes with nobody knowing — that's the same blind spot as March, just shorter.
Right. The health checks still look at the node, not at whether events are actually flowing end to end.
Which is exactly why we wanted the synthetic heartbeat. Where is that?
It's designed but not built. It's the same component as the customer-facing health panel, so it's slated for early June.
I'd push to pull it forward. I'm on calls with Brightpath and Summit Trust this month, and both asked how we'd detect a silent failure.
If I can't answer that with something real, it's going to cost us at renewal.
Okay. Chris, what would it take to ship the internal heartbeat by end of May and leave the customer UI for June?
If Ravi pairs with Sofia on it, probably two weeks. The UI is the long pole, not the heartbeat itself.
I can do that if we push the load-testing suite cleanup by a sprint.
I'm fine with that. Let's split it — internal heartbeat by May twenty-ninth, customer panel stays in June.
Scenario four was a bad config push, and rollback took four minutes, which is within target.
Scenario five was the one I was worried about — the circuit breaker payload threshold, the thing that hit Stratos Cloud in April.
With the new adaptive threshold it handled fifteen thousand events a minute without tripping, so that one's fixed.
Good, I'll let Damien's team know, they were really unhappy about that one.
Did we run anything on the shared clusters? Summit Trust and Crestline both had issues from the post-outage rebalancing.
Not in this round. That's a gap — we should add a noisy-neighbor scenario to the next game day.
Agreed. I'd like these game days to be quarterly, not a one-off.
I'll put it on the reliability sprint calendar and write it into the Q3 plan.
Can I get a customer-safe summary of today? Something I can share in renewal calls without exposing internals.
Yes. Ravi, draft the technical write-up, and Ananya, you turn it into the customer version.
Happy to. Honestly, this is the first time since March I feel like we have a good story.
Same. Great work, Ravi — this was a really solid game day.
Okay, actions: heartbeat by May twenty-ninth, a noisy-neighbor scenario next round, quarterly game days, and the two write-ups by Friday.
